title: What is Political Theory?

cards.h: Every question in Paper I starts here
cards.b:
Before you study Plato, Rawls or Marx, you need to know what "political theory" even is. UPSC asks about this directly, and the ideas here come back in almost every answer you write.

Political theory is the systematic thinking about political life. It asks big questions: Who should rule? Why should we obey? What is a just society? What is freedom?

Normative theory asks what should be. Plato's ideal state and Rawls's theory of justice are normative.

Empirical theory asks what is. It studies how voters actually behave or how parties actually win. David Easton and Robert Dahl worked this way.

Andrew Hacker

Political theory is a mix of two things: a search for knowledge about politics (science) and a search for the best political order (philosophy).

George Sabine

Political theory is "disciplined investigation of political problems". He saw it as the history of how thinkers answered the problems of their own times.

David Held

It is a network of concepts and generalisations about political life, covering ideas about government, state and society.

• Explain. It tells us why things happen, such as why revolutions break out.
  • Evaluate. It judges institutions against values, such as asking whether a law is just.
  • Prescribe. It suggests what we should do, such as how to make democracy deeper.

Good UPSC answers show all three. Don't only describe a thinker; say what their idea explains and where it falls short.

Political thought

The ideas of a person or a society at a given time, such as Gandhian thought.

Political philosophy

The most abstract level. It asks about the nature of the good life and of justice.

Political ideology

A set of ideas meant to drive action, such as liberalism or socialism. It wants to change the world, not just explain it.

Political science

The study of politics using scientific methods and data.
In the 1950s, many scholars said political theory was dying. Most new work was just history of old ideas, and the scientific study of politics was taking over.

David Easton, 1953

In The Political System, he said theory had become mere history of ideas. It was not producing new theory that could guide research.

Alfred Cobban, 1953

In his essay "The Decline of Political Theory", he blamed academics for turning away from real political problems.

Peter Laslett, 1956

He famously wrote that "for the moment, anyway, political philosophy is dead". He blamed logical positivism, which said value statements were meaningless.

Isaiah Berlin answered back in his 1962 essay "Does Political Theory Still Exist?". He said that as long as people disagree about ends, such as liberty vs equality, political theory will exist. Only in a world where everyone agreed on goals would it die.

"Political theory is a branch of moral philosophy."
Isaiah Berlin, Two Concepts of Liberty (1958)

Leo Strauss and Hannah Arendt also defended the classical tradition.

Then in 1971, John Rawls published A Theory of Justice. It is widely seen as the moment normative theory came roaring back.

cards.h: The end of ideology, history and old methods
cards.b:
Daniel Bell, 1960

In The End of Ideology, Bell argued that the West had settled its big ideological fights. Welfare capitalism had won, so grand political visions were exhausted. Critics said this was itself an ideology.

Quentin Skinner and the Cambridge School

Skinner's essay "Meaning and Understanding in the History of Ideas" (1969) said we must read old texts in their own context, as moves in the debates of their time. With J.G.A. Pocock and John Dunn, this gave the history of political thought new rigour.

Francis Fukuyama, 1989

His essay "The End of History?" (a book in 1992) claimed liberal democracy was the final form of government. Ethnic wars, 9/11 and China's rise showed the debate was far from over.

Indian debates show theory is alive. Think about reservation (equality vs merit), sedition law (order vs liberty), or the Uniform Civil Code (equality vs group rights).

Ambedkar's question in the Constituent Assembly, about political democracy without social democracy, is a normative question. Ending an answer with an Indian example like this lifts your marks.

Political theory asks what ought to be. That makes it hard to prove, because facts alone cannot settle a value question. David Hume made this point in A Treatise of Human Nature (1739–40). He argued that you cannot move from an "is" statement to an "ought" statement without some extra value premise. Scholars call this the is–ought gap.

  • Empirical: "Children in this village are underweight." This can be checked with data.
  • Normative: "The state must reduce child malnutrition." Data alone cannot prove this. You need a value, such as the right to health.

Why does this matter? A student who only lists facts has answered the empirical half. A good theory answer also argues why the state ought to act, and on which values.

Common exam trap: writing a long description of a theory and never giving a judgement. Theory questions usually ask you to evaluate, so end with your own reasoned view.

How it is asked. Prelims: you may be asked to tell normative from empirical statements. Mains: "Political theory is about what ought to be, not what is." Discuss.

"Comment: Political theory is dead." (a common style)
"Discuss the relevance of normative political theory today."

Structure: define theory, show the 1950s decline argument with names and years, show the revival through Berlin and Rawls, then end with how new areas like feminism, multiculturalism and green theory keep it alive.

quiz.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. In The Political System (1953), David Easton said political theory had become mere history of ideas.
2. Peter Laslett blamed logical positivism for holding that value statements were meaningful.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
quiz.w: 1 is true: Easton said theory had become mere history of ideas. 2 is false: Laslett blamed positivism for saying value statements were meaningless.

quiz.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Isaiah Berlin said political theory will exist as long as people disagree about ends such as liberty and equality.
2. John Rawls's A Theory of Justice (1971) is described as the book that ended the revival of normative theory.
3. Daniel Bell's The End of Ideology (1960) argued that the West had settled its big ideological fights.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
quiz.w: 1 is true: Berlin's test was disagreement about ends. 2 is false: Rawls's book is described as the start of the revival, not its end. 3 is true: Bell said the big ideological fights were settled.

quiz.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Quentin Skinner said old texts must be read in their own context, as moves in the debates of their time.
2. Francis Fukuyama's "The End of History?" claimed that ethnic wars and 9/11 proved liberal democracy was the final form of government.
3. George Sabine described political theory as "disciplined investigation of political problems".
How many of the statements given above are correct?
quiz.w: 1 is true: Skinner asked for reading texts in context. 2 is false: the lesson says those events showed the debate was far from over. 3 is true: Sabine's definition. Two are correct.

quiz.q:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Daniel Bell: The End of Ideology (1960)
2. Alfred Cobban: The Political System (1953)
3. Isaiah Berlin: "Meaning and Understanding in the History of Ideas" (1969)
How many pairs are correctly matched?
quiz.w: 1 is correct: Bell wrote The End of Ideology. 2 is wrong: The Political System is Easton's book; Cobban wrote The Decline of Political Theory. 3 is wrong: that 1969 essay is Skinner's, not Berlin's.

quiz.q:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Normative theory: asks what ought to be
2. Empirical theory: asks what ought to be
3. Political ideology: a set of ideas meant to drive action
How many pairs are correctly matched?
quiz.w: 1 is correct: normative theory asks what should be. 2 is wrong: empirical theory asks what is. 3 is correct: ideology is meant to drive action. Two are correct.

quiz.q:
Consider the following statements:
Statement-I: Berlin held that political theory could survive only in a world where everyone agreed on goals.
Statement-II: Berlin said political theory survives because people disagree about ends such as liberty and equality.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
o: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are individually true and Statement-II is the correct explanation of Statement-I
Both Statement-I and Statement-II are individually true but Statement-II is not the correct explanation of Statement-I
Statement-I is true but Statement-II is false
Statement-I is false but Statement-II is true
quiz.w: Statement-I is false: Berlin said theory would die only in a world where everyone agreed on goals. Statement-II is true: disagreement about ends is his reason for theory surviving.

quiz.q: Which one of the following is NOT one of the three jobs of political theory?
quiz.w: The three jobs are explain, evaluate and prescribe. Describe is not one of them.

quiz.q:
Arrange these in chronological order:
1. Peter Laslett's verdict that political philosophy was dead
2. John Rawls's A Theory of Justice
3. Isaiah Berlin's essay "Does Political Theory Still Exist?"
4. Daniel Bell's The End of Ideology
Which one of the following is the correct order?
quiz.w: Laslett 1956, then Bell 1960, Berlin 1962 and Rawls 1971. So 1-4-3-2.

quiz.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Normative theory asks what is, while empirical theory asks what ought to be.
2. George Sabine saw political theory as the history of how thinkers answered the problems of their own times.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
quiz.w: 1 is false: the lesson says the reverse; normative asks what should be and empirical asks what is. 2 is true: Sabine's view as the lesson describes it.

quiz.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Andrew Hacker described political theory as a mix of a search for knowledge about politics and a search for the best political order.
2. David Held described political theory only as the study of government, leaving out the state and society.
3. Ambedkar's question about political democracy without social democracy is a normative question.
How many of the statements given above are correct?
quiz.w: 1 is true: Hacker's mix of science and philosophy. 2 is false: Held's view covers government, state and society. 3 is true: the lesson calls it a normative question. Two are correct.

sources: Isaiah Berlin, 'Does Political Theory Still Exist?' (1962) and Two Concepts of Liberty (1958)
Peter Laslett (ed.), Philosophy, Politics and Society (1956)
Daniel Bell, The End of Ideology (1960); Quentin Skinner, History and Theory 8 (1969); Fukuyama, The National Interest (1989)
O.P. Gauba, An Introduction to Political Theory, ch. 1
PYQ themes: decline and resurgence of political theory (asked repeatedly in Paper I)
